Slavery in America. This was the forced labor system binding millions of people of African descent to perpetual servitude in the southern states from the sixteen-hundreds through 1865. It formed the economic foundation of the American South, structuring society, law, and culture around the enslavement of Black people for agricultural production. Slavery emerged gradually in colonial America during the sixteen-hundreds as planters in Virginia and the Carolinas shifted from indentured servitude to permanent racial slavery. It was justified by pseudoscientific racism and selective biblical interpretation that claimed Africans were inherently suited to enslavement. The slave trade generated vast wealth for southern planters and northern merchants, enriching Northern industrial development alongside Southern agriculture. This created fundamentally different economic and social systems, with the North industrializing while the South remained agrarian and rigidly hierarchical. As westward expansion proceeded, slavery sparked the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act, as the nation attempted and failed to manage slavery's expansion into new territories. These failures made the Civil War inevitable when the American political system could no longer contain the conflict between free and slave states. Slavery was abolished constitutionally by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865, yet its legacy persisted through Reconstruction's failure and the subsequent system of Jim Crow racial segregation, making the institution at the moral and political center of the war's causes and shaping American history long after its legal abolition.
